claims.text: Hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch.
Greater atomic-size mismatch produces greater lattice distortion.
Greater atomic-size mismatch leads to higher hardness and strength.
Homogenization and annealing eliminate compositional gradients in the proposed HEAs.
Atomic-size mismatch can be varied while holding the number of elements and overall compositional entropy constant.
The controlled comparison requires single-phase FCC or BCC solid solutions without significant precipitation or ordering.
Lattice distortion can be quantified using X-ray diffraction peak broadening or local-strain measurements.
Local lattice distortions caused by atomic-size mismatch act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Barriers created by local lattice distortions increase the critical resolved shear stress.
An increased critical resolved shear stress results in greater hardness and strength.
Under otherwise equal conditions, alloys with greater atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion will have higher hardness and strength than alloys with minimal mismatch.
HEAs composed of elements with similar atomic radii will have lower hardness and strength.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase HEAs without significant precipitation, ordering, or phase separation.
The hypothesis does not apply when secondary phases dominate mechanical properties.
Electronic effects and stacking-fault energy may also contribute significantly to HEA hardness and strength.
